hops.afterHeading: ABO: three alleles, two sugars and codominance
hops.title: Gut-bacterial enzymes that turn type A blood into type O
hops.text: In a 2019 paper, a University of British Columbia team seeking more universal-donor blood searched somewhere unlikely: DNA from the feces of a donor with type AB blood. Why the gut? Its lining carries sugars much like the blood-group ones, and some gut bacteria feed on them. In the ABO system, a type A red cell differs from a type O cell by one extra sugar, N-acetylgalactosamine, on its H antigen. From 19,500 pieces of gut-bacterial DNA, they found two enzymes from the bacterium Flavonifractor plautii that work together, one altering that sugar, the other removing it. In whole blood, the treated red cells typed as group O.

sources.citation: Rahfeld et al., An enzymatic pathway in the human gut microbiome that converts A to universal O type blood, Nature Microbiology 4:1475-1485 (2019)
Rahfeld and Withers, Toward universal donor blood: enzymatic conversion of A and B to O type, Journal of Biological Chemistry 295:325-334 (2020)
University of British Columbia news, Gut enzymes could hold key to producing universal blood (21 August 2018)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A lab bench with a petri dish of small bacterial colonies next to a rack of test tubes holding red blood.
image.caption: Two enzymes from a gut bacterium remove the A sugar from red cells, so the cells type as O.

hops.title: Why hairless dogs keep having fluffy puppies
hops.text: Mate two hairless Chinese Crested dogs and some of the puppies arrive in a full, soft coat. Breeders call these pups powderpuffs, and they keep turning up. Chinese Cresteds, Mexican hairless dogs and Peruvian hairless dogs all share the same seven-base duplication in a gene called FOXI3, which helps build hair and teeth. Dogs with one copy have little or no hair and often missing or oddly shaped teeth. No copies gives a powderpuff. Two copies stop development very early in pregnancy, so that class is never born, and among live pups you expect about two hairless for every powderpuff. The hairless type can never breed true.

sources.citation: Online Mendelian Inheritance in Animals, Ectodermal dysplasia, FOXI3-related, in dog (OMIA 000323-9615), University of Sydney
Kupczik et al., Canine FOXI3 mutation and dental development, Scientific Reports 7:5459 (2017)
Drogemuller et al., A mutation in hairless dogs implicates FOXI3 in ectodermal development, Science 321:1462 (2008)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Two hairless Chinese Crested dogs on a rug beside two hairless puppies and one fluffy long-haired puppy.
image.caption: Two copies of the hairless allele are lethal, so hairless parents keep having fluffy powderpuff pups.

hops.title: Eye color is not a one-gene trait
hops.text: Eye color was long taught as a one-gene trait: brown dominant, blue recessive, so two blue-eyed parents could never have a brown-eyed child. Many genes influence eye color, and several of them affect how much pigment builds up in the iris. The two biggest players sit side by side on chromosome 15. OCA2 helps make melanin, the pigment in the iris. A switch tucked inside its neighbor, HERC2, sets how much OCA2 the iris makes, and the version linked to blue eyes turns it down. Because other pigment genes also weigh in, the old rule fails: although it is uncommon, two blue-eyed parents can have a brown-eyed child.

sources.citation: White and Rabago-Smith, Genotype-phenotype associations and human eye color, Journal of Human Genetics 56:5-7 (2011)
Sturm et al., A single SNP in an evolutionary conserved region within intron 86 of the HERC2 gene determines human blue-brown eye color, American Journal of Human Genetics 82:424-431 (2008)
MedlinePlus Genetics, Is eye color determined by genetics? U.S. National Library of Medicine

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A row of glass marbles on a windowsill shading from pale blue through green and hazel to dark brown.
image.caption: Many interacting genes set iris pigment, so eye color does not follow a simple one-gene dominant rule.
